title: Look at the thing
hookLine: look at the thing itself and do it steadily, kindly, modestly (Meditations 8.5)

cards: A carpenter is fitting a door. The house is noisy, the client is hovering, his phone keeps buzzing, and there's a radio talking about the end of the world. None of it changes the door.
The hinge still has to sit flush; the gap still has to be even. A good carpenter's eyes stay on the wood. Most days, eyes wander everywhere except the work in front of them.
In book eight, Marcus Aurelius tells himself where to look.

teach.b: Meditations eight, five, begins by telling Marcus not to be disturbed, because everything happens according to the nature of the whole, and in a little while he'll be nobody and nowhere, like the emperors Hadrian and Augustus before him.
That's the radio switched off, big worries put back to their actual size.

teach.h: FIX YOUR EYES ON THE MATTER.
teach.b: Then, he says, fix your eyes on the matter in front of you and look at it. Just that. See the actual task, not your feelings about it, not the story of how it'll go.
Struggles with work often start because no one really looks at the thing; they look at the dread around it.
While you look, keep in mind that your duty is to be a good human being, and do what human nature asks without turning aside.
Then the manner: speak and act as seems most just to you, but do it with kindness, with modesty, and without pretense. Not just correctly; kindly. Not just firmly; modestly.
Notice how calm that whole sequence is. Turn down the noise. Look at the thing.
Remember who you're trying to be.
Do it steadily and gently. That's not a heroic program. It's a carpenter's program, and it works on a spreadsheet, a diaper, a hard email, a door.

how: Readers of Marcus often use 8.5 as a short routine before difficult work: set aside big worries, look plainly at the task itself, and do it steadily and kindly.

o: a builder who ignores people to finish the job fast
Marcus's picture for looking straight at the task in hand
a Roman trade Marcus took up to keep himself humble

games.q: look at the thing — tap the pairs.
p: on the matter in front of you

s: 8.5 names Hadrian and Augustus to shrink Marcus's worries
in a little while he'll be nobody and nowhere, like them.
Marcus says doing the task correctly is enough, whatever the manner
he adds kindness, modesty and no pretense.

games.q: you're dreading a hard email and keep circling it. by 8.5, what's the next move?
o: look plainly at what the email needs, and write it kindly and steadily.
send something quick to get it over with.
games.why: Meditations 8.5: fix your eyes on the matter, remember your duty to be good, and act with kindness, modesty and without pretense.

practice: Bring to mind one task waiting for you, not the dread of it, the task itself: what exactly is it, and where would your hands be on the first step? See it plainly, the way a carpenter sees the hinge.
Then picture doing it slowly, steadily, kindly to anyone involved.

wordCard.voice: Carpenter. Marcus's picture for looking straight at the task: the carpenter whose eyes stay on the wood, kindly and steadily. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: steadily. Whatever the thing is, it gets a little better when someone finally looks at it. Until tomorrow.
